paper_title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become central recipe for improving reasoning-oriented LLMs, using verifier to score sampled solutions and optimize the policy based on the resulting scores [18, 9, 28, 16]. This paradigm is most straightforward when the reward is complete: the verifier can reliably determine whether each sampled solution is correct. Outside curated training environments, however, constructing such complete verifiers becomes bottleneck. Users may specify task without being able to provide full checker, and in open-ended scientific or reasoning domains, certifying proposed answer can be as difficult as producing one. The central 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Figure 2: Illustration of one-sided verifiability across executable checks, constraint checks, and LLM-as-verifier settings. rejection provides concrete evidence of failure, whereas acceptance only means that no checked violation was found; it does not certify correctness. question is therefore not only how to learn from verifiable rewards, but how to learn when verification itself is incomplete. The key observation of this paper is that incomplete verification is often asymmetric. Complete correctness may be unavailable, expensive, or as hard as solving the task, while local failures are much easier to detect. For example, in code generation, failing unit test exposes concrete bug even though passing test suite does not establish full program correctness [3, 24, 37]. In structured reasoning tasks, explicit format or domain constraints can reject invalid answers without solving the task [23]. When no reliable task-specific checker is available, an LLM verifier may still identify obvious flaws in proposed solution [4, 44, 40]. As illustrated in Figure 2, these checks provide one-sided evidence: rejection is high-confidence evidence of failure, whereas an acceptance only means that no checked violation was found. We study this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verifier-negative judgments have high precision, while verifier-positive judgments may contain non-negligible false-positive component. Under OSV, reward of 0 is high-confidence negative evidence, but reward of 1 is not trusted positive label and only non-falsified candidate. Existing approaches do not directly address this regime. Verifier-free or self-training methods construct surrogate learning signals from majority agreement, novelty, or confidence-like statistics [47, 45, 1, 36]. These methods show that useful signals can be obtained without ground-truth labels, but they do not exploit common form of external feedback: reliable rejection without reliable acceptance. Conversely, standard RLVR methods such as GRPO [30] use the available verifier as binary reward, reinforcing verifier-positive samples and suppressing verifier-negative samples. Under OSV, this binary interpretation is misleading. False positives are not merely noisy evaluations; once used as rewards, they become attractors of the policy optimization dynamics. Shortcut solutions that exploit unchecked failure modes receive direct positive gradients whenever they pass the partial verifier, allowing the policy to improve verifier pass rate without improving true correctness [33, 13]. In this paper, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), policy optimization method designed for one-sided verifiable rewards. NOPO uses the verifier only for the evidence it can safely provide: high-confidence negatives. It suppresses verifier-negative trajectories while treating verifier-positive trajectories as unlabeled rather than correct. This negative-only principle creates new optimization challenge: suppressing failures redistributes probability mass, but an all-failed rollout group provides no grounded direction for where that mass should move. NOPO addresses this challenge with two safeguards. At the sample level, it uses reference-relative NPO loss whose gradient self-attenuates once verifier-negative response is sufficiently downweighted relative to the reference policy. At the group level, it scales negative updates by the amount of non-falsified support in the same rollout group. Importantly, this support weight does not treat verifier-positive samples as correct demonstrations; it uses only their aggregate count to indicate whether the current policy has produced non-falsified alternatives toward which probability mass can be conservatively redistributed. Together, these components enable policy improvement from reliable negative evidence without directly reinforcing noisy positives. 2 Our main contributions are: 1. One-sided verifiability. We identify and formalize common regime in realistic LLM tasks where local falsification is reliable but complete verification is unavailable. Under OSV, verifier negatives provide high-confidence evidence of failure, whereas verifier positives are only nonfalsified candidates rather than trusted positive labels. 2. Negative-Only Policy Optimization. We propose NOPO, an RL method that learns from highconfidence negatives without directly reinforcing noisy positives. NOPO combines sample-level reference-relative NPO suppression with group-level non-falsified support weight, yielding conservative policy improvement under one-sided verifiable rewards. 3. Empirical validation. We validate the OSV noise profile across multiple verifier types, showing that negative judgments are substantially cleaner than positive judgments. Under OSV, NOPO improves the models capability frontier over standard RLVR baselines, and the gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

sections.title: 3 One-Sided Verifiability
sections.content: 3.1 Verifier Model and Examples In the unsupervised RLVR setting [47, 10], the true correctness of sampled solutions is unobserved during training, so rewards must be constructed. Prior work derives rewards from model-internal or sample-level statistics, including agreement among sampled outputs [47] and verifier-free uncertainty objectives such as entropy minimization [1]. We study different yet common supervision source: manually specified error-detecting checks. Such checks are often easy to define when full correctness is hard to verify, because they test necessary conditions rather than correctness itself. Failing check provides evidence that solution is wrong, whereas passing the available checks only indicates that no checked failure mode was detected. Let denote problem instance and complete candidate solution. We distinguish between the latent ground-truth correctness r(x, y) {0, 1}, and the observed reward r(x, y) = (x, y) {0, 1}, where denotes manually specified error-detection scheme available at training time. Such schemes are easy to obtain in many settings. We describe three common instances below. Executable checks. properties of solution. The central question in this paper is not how to eliminate verifier noise completely, but how to perform RL when the available signal can reliably falsify some bad solutions but cannot reliably certify good ones. 3.2 Measuring One-Sidedness We measure this asymmetry with two conditional quantities: qneg := Pr(r = 0 = 0), qpos := Pr(r = 0 = 1). (7) (8) These quantities measure the probability that the ground-truth reward is false under each observed reward outcome: qneg is the probability that verifier-negative sample is truly incorrect, and qpos is the probability that verifier-positive sample is nevertheless incorrect. We call verifier one-sided verifiable when qneg is high but qpos remains non-negligible. In this regime, observed negatives can be used as trusted counterexamples, whereas observed positives should be treated as non-falsified unlabeled candidates rather than ground-truth positives. For the LLM self-verifier, qneg is close to 1, showing accurate error identification with few rejected correct answers. sections.title: 4 Negative-Only Policy Optimization
sections.content: In the one-sided verifiable rewards (OSV) setting, the reliability of verifier-positive samples is generally unknown: qpos is difficult to observe in realistic training environments. We therefore learn only from the reliable side of the signal, namely verifier-negative samples. This principle resembles Negative Preference Optimization (NPO), introduced in the preliminaries. NPO-style unlearning methods aim to reduce the likelihood of specified undesirable examples or behaviors relative to reference policy, while preserving the models original capabilities. 5 However, NPO-style algorithms are typically designed for off-policy updates on fixed negative dataset, unlike on-policy RLVR. With fixed negatives, NPO suppresses undesirable examples relative to reference policy and stops once their likelihood is sufficiently reduced. In RLVR, however, negatives are generated online by the changing policy itself. Negative-only updates therefore face group-level ambiguity: suppressing rejected trajectories redistributes probability mass, but verifiernegative samples alone do not specify where it should move. Overly aggressive suppression can induce unconstrained move-away updates, causing the policy to generate new failures that are then further suppressed. Directly applying NPO is therefore insufficient for OSV-based RL training. Although the NPO loss provides sample-level self-attenuation relative to the reference policy, it does not distinguish whether verifier-negative rollout comes from group that also contains non-falsified responses. This distinction is important in on-policy RLVR: when the same rollout group contains non-falsified responses, suppressing clear failures is more likely to redistribute probability mass toward the non-falsified part of the sampled group. To adapt NPO to this setting, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which modulates NPO suppression by the amount of non-falsified support in the same rollout group. Importantly, verifier-positive samples are not treated as correct demonstrations. NOPO uses only their aggregate count as support signal, indicating whether the current policy has produced non-falsified responses under the available verifier. Non-falsified support weight. Given prompt x, let = (y1, . . . , yG) be rollout group sampled from the old policy πθold ( x), and let ri = (x, yi) {0, 1} denote the verifier label of the i-th rollout. We define the amount of non-falsified support in the group as c(r) := (cid:88) i=1 ri, (9) where = (r1, . . . , rG). If c(r) = 0, the rollout group contains no non-falsified response under the available verifier, and negative-only suppression provides little information about useful direction for probability redistribution. This event is common on hard prompts: under the rollout distribution, Pr[c(r) = 0] equals one minus the verifier-pass@G rate, namely the probability that none of the sampled responses passes the available verifier checks. NOPO therefore weights each negative update by the non-falsified support within its rollout group: ωγ(r) := 1, (cid:18) c(r) (cid:19)γ γ = 0, , γ > 0, γ 0. (10) The default γ = 1 gives linear support weight. When γ > 0, groups with no verifier-positive responses receive zero weight automatically, low-support groups contribute less, and groups with more non-falsified support allow stronger suppression of verifier-negative responses. Setting γ = 0 recovers vanilla NPO, where all groups contribute uniformly, while larger γ makes NOPO more conservative on low-support groups. The resulting NOPO objective applies NPO-style suppression only to verifier-negative responses, modulated by the group-level non-falsified support weight: LNOPO(θ) = ExD,yπθold (x) ωγ(r) (cid:34) (cid:35) I[ri = 0] LNPO(θ; x, yi) , (11) 1 G (cid:88) i=1 where ri = (x, yi) and LNPO is the reference-relative NPO loss with temperature β. The verifier labels and the support weight are treated as fixed feedback for the sampled rollout group; gradients are applied only through the NPO loss on verifier-negative responses. Algorithm 1 in Appendix summarizes the corresponding training update. This formulation separates reliability at two levels. The NPO term provides sample-level control: its gradient self-attenuates once the current policy assigns negative response lower probability than the reference. The group weight ωγ(r) provides group-level control: it trusts negative evidence only when the same on-policy rollout group contains verifier-positive support. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: 5.1 Setup We use Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as base models [38]. Code experiments cover LiveCodeBench [15], TACO test [20], and CodeContests [21] with public-test binary rewards, with CodeForces reserved as an unseen cross-benchmark transfer target. Logic experiments use ZebraLogic with deterministic constraint checker that verifies format and domain constraints without certifying full correctness, while math experiments use OlympiadBench [11] with an LLM self-verifier binary reward. We compare four methods, each using = 16 samples per prompt: GRPO, which directly optimizes the observed verifier reward; EM-RL, token-level verifier-free baseline that minimizes policy entropy during training [1]; w-Reinforce, which assigns verifier-negative samples greater weight than positive ones [46]; and NOPO, our proposed method. 5.2 Main Result As shown in Table 2, NOPO achieves the best average pass@16 on both backbones among RL methods, with w-Reinforce second on average. Both methods treat verifier-negative samples as trustworthy supervision but differ in how they control policy drift from negative-only penalties: w-Reinforce gives verifier-positive samples small positive weight to offset the dominant negative gradient, whereas NOPO directly rescales each prompts negative-only loss by its within-group non-falsified support. By contrast, verifier-free EM-RL, which uses only token-level entropy minimization, gives essentially no gain over Base on either backbone, consistent with the view that intrinsic-reward methods are bounded by sharpening the base policys initial distribution [1, 43, 39, 10]. At the per-cell level, NOPO ranks first in 9 of 10 benchmarkbackbone cells; the only exception is OlympiadBench under Qwen3-8B, where it ranks second behind GRPO. As Table 1 shows, OlympiadBench has the lowest verifier negative-class recall in our setup, so few truly incorrect rollouts are flagged, weakening NOPOs negative-only supervision signal. 5.3 Inference-Time Scaling central debate around RLVR is whether it expands models capability frontier [25] or merely concentrates probability mass on solutions already discoverable at large [39, 45]. We therefore test whether our gains persist at large inference budgets, rather than reflecting sharpening around solutions reachable by the base model with enough samples. Table 3 reports Qwen3-4B on CodeContests and LiveCodeBench as scales from 1 to 512. NOPO shows an advantage at larger inference budgets, and this advantage widens with k, indicating genuine frontier expansion: the post-RL policy solves problems the base model cannot reach even with hundreds of attempts. w-Reinforce, which also suppresses verifier-negative outputs, is the consistent runner-up at large k, supporting the OSV view that trusted-negative suppression drives frontier expansion. NOPOs per-prompt non-falsified support weight further improves on this principle. GRPO, by contrast, illustrates the sharpening failure mode: its pass@1 is the highest across methods, but at = 512 it falls below the base model on both benchmarks, indicating that small-k gains come at the cost of exploration. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Unsupervised RLVR. Unsupervised RLVR can be categorized into two regimes by reward source [10]. The intrinsic regime derives rewards from the model itself through certaintyor consistency-based signals [47, 22, 1, 45, 43, 12], and is provably bounded by the sharpening of the policys initial distribution. The external regime grounds rewards in mechanisms outside the model and typically relies on verifiers that are effectively sound and complete, such as formal proof checkers, deterministic execution against complete test suites, or exact symbolic checks [14, 42, 32]. Our setting falls within this external regime but relaxes its soundness-and-completeness assumption: readily available external verifiers in realistic deployment settings often cannot certify correctness, but can reliably reject visible failures, an asymmetry we formalize as one-sided verifiability. RLVR with Noisy Rewards. growing line of work studies RLVR when the verifier is imperfect [29, 2, 5], and existing methods share common recipe: characterize the verifiers noiseeither through an aggregate quality index or through separately modeled false-positive and false-negative ratesand plug this characterization into the policy gradient as correction or weighting term. Obtaining such characterization itself requires ground-truth labels for calibration, which our setting explicitly disallows; moreover, the rate at which the verifier falsely accepts incorrect outputs drifts upward as the policy learns to satisfy partial checks, so calibrated pre-training estimates or online noise-rate estimates may be unreliable in the OSV regime. NOPO instead works structurally rather than statistically: it neither estimates nor corrects for noise rates, using the verifier only for the highconfidence negatives it can safely provide, consistent with the broader observation that false-positive rewards are particularly harmful as they reinforce shortcut behaviors [13]. Negative-Oriented Optimization. NOPO is also related to negative-oriented optimization. LLM unlearning removes undesirable knowledge or behaviors while preserving general utility [6, 26, 19]. Negative preference objectives such as NPO suppress fixed off-policy forget set while avoiding naive gradient-ascent instability, with later variants revisiting the reference model [41, 7]. NOPO adopts NPOs self-attenuating suppression principle but applies it to on-policy verifier-negative rollouts, which introduces redistribution ambiguity: negatives specify what to avoid, not where probability mass should move. This motivates our group-level non-falsified support gate. Another related line, negative sample reinforcement in RLVR, shows that penalizing incorrect rollouts can improve reasoning and preserve diversity [46, 34, 27, 8]. Unlike these methods, NOPO targets OSV, where verifier positives are unlabeled non-falsified support rather than reliable positive rewards.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: As LLM capabilities improve and their applications expand, constructing complete verifiers for increasingly diverse training data becomes increasingly costly. This paper studies more practical setting where only partial verification is available. We show that verifier rewards in this setting often exhibit one-sided verifiability: rejected samples provide reliable evidence of failure, whereas accepted samples are merely non-falsified rather than certified correct. Under this asymmetry, directly treating verifier-positive samples as positive rewards introduces substantial noise and may encourage reward hacking rather than expand the models true capability frontier. We therefore propose NegativeOnly Policy Optimization (NOPO), which learns only from high-confidence negative evidence. NOPO combines sample-level reference-relative NPO suppression with group-level non-falsified support weighting, enabling controlled negative updates without directly reinforcing noisy positives. Empirically, NOPO improves performance across multiple verifier types, with advantages that persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer. These results suggest that properly leveraging negative evidence can substantially expand the models capability frontier without groundtruth verifiers, making negative-only optimization promising direction for scalable RLVR. Limitations. Negative-only learning is inherently delicate: it specifies what the policy should avoid but not where removed probability mass should move. This limitation motivates NOPOs conservative design and suggests future extensions. In different one-sided verifiability scenarios, verifier-positive samples may contain exploitable structure, such as pairwise comparisons or uncertainty-based filtering, that could yield partial positive signals. Incorporating such signals while preserving the robustness of negative-only optimization remains an important direction for future work.

sections.title: C Experimental Details
sections.content: C.1 Benchmark All datasets involved are publicly available. For LiveCodeBench, we use the code-generation split of release_v6. For TACO, we use the evaluation set released by TCS [37] and exclude 64 problems for which our parser cannot extract public test cases. For CodeContests, we use the evaluation set released by CURE [35]. For ZebraLogic, we use the Medium-Large subset (4 4, 4 5, 5 3, and 62). Unless otherwise specified above, datasets are used as provided. For the main results in Table 2, training and evaluation use the same test set for each benchmark, whereas the transfer experiments in Table 4 evaluate on target benchmarks not used for training. Only one-sided verifier rewards are available during training, and all methods are evaluated using the oracle. Table 5 summarizes the training verifiers and evaluation oracles. Table 5: Training rewards, evaluation oracles, and mean test counts per problem. Benchmark Training reward Evaluation oracle Tests: OSV / oracle public-test binary reward TACO public-test binary reward CodeContests public-test binary reward LCB ZebraLogic constraint checker OlympiadBench LLM self-verifier full test suite (public + hidden) 1.7 / 204 full test suite (public + hidden) 1.9 / 12 full test suite (public + hidden) 2.6 / 40 ground-truth answer ground-truth answer C.2 Experimental Configuration All RL runs use the verl framework [31] with vLLM rollouts [17] and an FSDP actor. The two backbones are Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode. Unless noted otherwise, every method shares the optimisation, sampling, and bookkeeping settings below; only the loss term and its method-specific hyperparameter change between methods. 14 Optimisation. We use AdamW with constant learning rate of 5 107 after 20-step linear warmup. The training batch is 16 prompts; each prompt produces = 16 on-policy rollouts, giving 1616 = 256-rollout step. PPO mini-batches contain 4 prompts and we run single inner PPO epoch per global step. The maximum number of global steps is 150. For all methods dominated by negative optimisation, prolonged training may lead to entropy divergence, so we monitor policy entropy during training and retain the most recent checkpoint saved before an observed entropy divergence for evaluation. Sampling. single sampling profile is shared between RL rollouts and validation rollouts. For Qwen3 models in non-thinking mode, generation uses temperature=0.8, top_p=0.8, top_k=20, and min_p=0. Sequence lengths. Code experiments use max_response_length=8192. Logic and math experiments use max_response_length=16384. Method-specific hyperparameters. GRPO: kl_loss_coef=103, no other deviations from the verl default. w-Reinforce [46]: verifier-positive samples receive weight λ = 0.1, verifier-negative samples receive weight 1. EM-RL [1]: adv_estimator=rloo; the training reward is replaced by token-level entropy minimisation computed inside the trainer from actor log-probabilities, and the environment reward manager returns zero placeholders on the training path. Validation still routes through the task-native evaluator so pass@k is reported on the same scale as the other methods. NPO: β = 0.1, kl_loss_coef=0. The reference policy πref is the frozen base model. NOPO (default): β = 0.1, γ = 1.0, kl_loss_coef=0. The non-falsified support weight ωγ(r) from Eq. 10 is computed from the same on-policy rollout group used for the NPO term; c(r)=0 groups receive zero weight automatically and are dropped from the actor update. Inference-time scaling. For the inference-scaling sweep  (Table 3)  , we resample = 512 rollouts per problem from each methods checkpoint with the same sampling profile and report pass@k as function of {1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512}. Compute resources. All RL training runs were executed on eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80GB memory per GPU. typical (method, backbone, benchmark) run takes approximately 12 hours under this setup. Evaluation-only sweeps reuse selected checkpoints and are cheaper than training, although the inference-time scaling results in Table 3 require generating up to 512 rollouts per problem and still take approximately 12 hours under the same configuration. Per-target ablation numbers Table 6 expands Figure 4 with per-target pass@16 for the five-method ablation on Qwen3-4B trained on TACO. Train is in-domain pass@16; the remaining columns are unseen-transfer pass@16 (G = 16 inference samples per problem) for the same selected checkpoint. Unseen-Avg is the macro mean of the three unseen-transfer columns and matches the right-hand bars of Figure 4. Bold marks the column maximum. sections.title: G Verifier characteristics and NOPO gains
sections.content: Table 9 compares verifier asymmetry with NOPOs pass@16 gains over GRPO across all ten settings. NOPO improves over GRPO at both extremes of qpos (19.777.5%): non-falsified support scales negative updates rather than directly reinforcing verifier-positive responses. The clearest association is with negative recall: NOPO gains 2.956.72 points in the eight code/logic settings, where verifiers detect at least third of true failures. On OlympiadBench, recall is only 913%, leaving few trusted negatives and reducing the NOPOGRPO margins to +0.89 and 0.45 points.

sections.title: H Comparison with NPO
sections.content: Table 10 extends the NPO comparison to all five benchmarks on Qwen3-8B under the main experimental protocol. NOPO improves over NPO, the γ = 0 special case of Eq. 10, on every benchmark by 1.194.37 points, supporting the contribution of the non-falsified support weight. NPO also outperforms GRPO on average (49.35 versus 48.27). For rollout group with verifier-negative fraction p, the total suppression weight before the common 1/G normalization scales as pG for NPO and p(1 p)G for NOPO with γ = 1. NPO therefore applies the largest suppression to all-failed groups, whereas NOPOs weight is maximal for mixed groups and vanishes at both extremes. For example, groups with 80% and 20% negative rollouts receive equal total weight under NOPO, while NPO assigns four times as much to the former. 16 Table 9: Pre-RL verifier statistics and the NOPOGRPO pass@16 gap. sections.title: I Verifier Implementation Details
sections.content: This section specifies the two non-trivial verifiers used in the main results: the ZebraLogic constraintcheck verifier (Section I.1) and the LLM self-verifier on OlympiadBench (Section I.2). I.1 Constraint-Check Verifier on ZebraLogic ZebraLogic puzzles ask the model to assign 1 features to houses subject to list of naturallanguage clues; the gold solution is JSON object {"header": [...], "rows": [[...]]} with exactly rows. Our verifier checks whether the candidate assignment satisfies the puzzles schema and domain constraints necessary conditions induced by the task specification without consulting the clues or the gold assignment. I.2 LLM Self-Verifier on OlympiadBench For OlympiadBench, the policy and the verifier use the same Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B backbone in non-thinking mode. Three-turn audit prompt. For each rollout we send three-turn chat: 1. user: the original problem statement, with the standard instruction Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. 2. assistant: the candidate solution emitted by the policy. 3. user: the verification instruction shown below, which asks the verifier to search the existing reasoning for concrete mathematical errors and emit final-line trailer of the form Is the existing reasoning correct (Yes/No)? X. The instruction explicitly tells the verifier not to demand proof completeness and to output No only when it finds concrete answer-changing mathematical error deliberate design choice that makes the verifier behave as falsifier rather than certifier. 17 Prompt Template for the LLM Self-Verifier [User] {QUESTION} [Assistant] {CANDIDATE_REASONING_OR_SOLUTION} [User] You are skeptical but fair math verifier. Audit the student's solution for concrete mathematical errors, not for proof completeness. Look for: - arithmetic mistakes, - invalid algebraic transformations, - misuse of formula or theorem, - omitted cases or ignored constraints only when you can name concrete alternative case that changes the final answer, - final answer that contradicts the preceding work or relies on demonstrably false step. Do not mark solution wrong for style, brevity, missing explanatory prose, incomplete rigor, or failure to prove optimality, unless you can identify concrete counterexample or specific answer-changing mathematical error. Verdict policy: - If you find at least one specific answer-changing error, judge No. - If the final answer is correct and the computations used are correct, judge Yes even if the proof is incomplete. - If suspected issue is ambiguous, judge Yes rather than hallucinating an error. At the end of your response, on new line, write exactly: "Is the existing reasoning correct (Yes/No)? X" where is either Yes or No.
